verses.text: Chrysaor fathered three-headed Geryon
after mating with Callirhoe, daughter of famous Oceanus.
Mighty Heracles killed Geryon
beside his shambling cattle on Erytheia, surrounded by water,
on the day he drove the broad-browed cattle
to sacred Tiryns, crossing the stream of Oceanus,
after killing Orthus and Eurytion the cattle herder
in their misty cattle shelter beyond famous Oceanus.
Ceto bore another monster, impossible to overcome, nothing like
mortal humans or the deathless gods:
divine, fierce-hearted Echidna, born in a hollow cave,
half a bright-eyed nymph with lovely cheeks,
and half a monstrous snake, dreadful and huge,
with dappled skin, eating raw flesh in the depths of sacred earth.
There her cave lies deep beneath a hollow rock,
far from deathless gods and mortal humans.
There the gods assigned her a splendid home to live in.
There dreadful Echidna stays underground in the land of the Arimoi,
a nymph who never dies or grows old, through all her days.
They say Typhaon joined in love with Echidna,
he, terrible, violent and lawless, with that bright-eyed girl.
She became pregnant and bore fierce-hearted children.
First she bore Orthus, a dog for Geryon;
second she bore a monster beyond words, impossible to overcome:
Cerberus, the raw-flesh-eating dog of Hades, with a voice like bronze,
with fifty heads, merciless and strong.
Third she bore the Hydra, skilled in deadly harm,
the water snake of Lerna, whom white-armed Hera raised,
her anger at mighty Heracles knowing no bounds.
But Zeus's son killed the Hydra with pitiless bronze,
Amphitryon's son, together with Iolaus, who loved battle,
Heracles, guided by Athena, bringer of spoils.
Echidna also bore the Chimera, breathing unstoppable fire,
dreadful and huge, swift-footed and strong.
She had three heads: one a fierce-eyed lion's,
one a goat's, and one a snake's, a mighty serpent's.
A lion in front, a serpent behind, a goat in the middle,
she breathed out the dreadful force of blazing fire.
Pegasus and brave Bellerophon brought her down.
Echidna bore the deadly Sphinx, a curse on the people of Thebes,
after mating with Orthus, and also the lion of Nemea.
Hera, Zeus's glorious wife, raised the lion
and settled him in Nemea's hills, a curse on humans.
Living there, he ravaged the local people,
ruling over Tretus, Nemea and Apesas.
But mighty Heracles overpowered him with his strength.
Ceto joined in love with Phorcys and bore her youngest child,
a dreadful snake that, in the hidden depths of dark earth,
at its vast outer limits, guards the all-golden apples.
Such are the offspring of Ceto and Phorcys.

uncertainties: Verse 295 names the mother only as 'she'; Ceto is a common interpretation, but Callirhoe is also possible.
In verse 326, 'she' may refer to Echidna or the Chimera. This translation follows the earlier draft in choosing Echidna.
Verses 323–324 are marked for deletion in the supplied Greek. They are translated here because every assigned verse was requested.
Athena's title in verse 318 has a disputed meaning; 'bringer of spoils' is a traditional interpretation.
